body.stem: You have a Recovery Services vault that protects a production Linux virtual machine with an Azure Virtual Machine backup policy. The VM was created from a Trusted Launch image and has Ultra Disk and Premium SSD v2 data disks attached; the scheduled backup jobs are failing because those disk types are not supported by the current configuration. The business wants the workload protected more than once a day and wants rapid restore points to remain available for a full week. You need to update the backup policy in the vault. Which change should you make?

exhibit.text:
Recovery Services vault                : rsv-prod-01
Protected item                        : vm-app-01 (Linux, Trusted Launch image)
Attached data disks                   : 2 x Ultra Disk (512 GiB each), 1 x Premium SSD v2
Policy subtype                        : Standard
Backup frequency                      : Daily
Retention range (daily recovery pts)  : 180 days
Instant Restore snapshot retention    : 7 days

options.text: Change the policy subtype to Enhanced and change the backup frequency to Hourly
Change the policy subtype to Enhanced and change the Instant Restore snapshot retention to 1 day
Keep the policy subtype as Standard and change the backup frequency to Hourly
Keep the policy subtype as Standard and change the retention range for daily recovery points to 10 years

explanation.correct: The failing jobs are caused by the disk types on the VM: the Standard policy subtype cannot protect Ultra Disk or Premium SSD v2, while the Enhanced subtype adds support for Ultra Disks, Premium SSD v2 and Trusted Launch VMs, and it also brings zone-redundant Instant Restore snapshots plus the ability to schedule backups as often as every 4 hours. Moving the frequency to Hourly therefore both clears the unsupported-disk failures and delivers more than one backup per day, and it leaves the existing 7-day Instant Restore snapshot retention untouched, which already satisfies the one-week rapid restore requirement. Note also that once a VM is protected with the Enhanced subtype, it cannot be moved back to Standard.

perChoice.b: Changing the subtype to Enhanced fixes the unsupported disk types, but shortening the Instant Restore snapshot retention from 7 days to 1 day breaks the requirement that rapid restore points stay available for a week, and the frequency is left unchanged, so the workload is still protected only once a day. Instant Restore snapshot retention can be set anywhere from 1 to 30 days and already defaults to 7 days, so no reduction is needed here.
perChoice.c: Keeping the Standard subtype leaves the backup jobs failing, because Standard cannot protect Ultra Disk or Premium SSD v2. Backing up Trusted Launch VMs with Standard is only possible through Azure CLI 2.73.0 or later, PowerShell Az 14.0.0 or later, or the REST API 2025-01-01 or later, and none of that changes the unsupported disk types. Changing the frequency alone does not resolve the failures.
perChoice.d: Retention length governs how long recovery points are kept; it does not change which disk types can be protected. With the Standard subtype the Ultra Disk and Premium SSD v2 remain uncovered and the jobs keep failing, and the once-a-day schedule is left in place. Longer retention also does not create extra backup runs per day.

body.stem: You have a Recovery Services vault that protects several Azure virtual machines with an Azure Virtual Machine backup policy. The business rule for this workload requires that daily recovery points are kept for three months, and the application team wants the recovery points that support a fast restore to remain available for two weeks after each backup. You need to update the policy in the vault so that both requirements are met. Which change should you make?

rows: Retention range for daily recovery points

options.text: Raise the retention range for daily recovery points to 90 days and then set Instant Restore retention to 14 days.
Set Instant Restore retention to 14 days while leaving the retention range for daily recovery points at 7 days.
Raise the retention range for daily recovery points to 90 days and set Instant Restore retention to 45 days.
Raise the retention range for daily recovery points to 14 days and leave Instant Restore retention at 7 days.

explanation.correct: For an Enhanced policy the Instant Restore snapshot retention can be set from 1 to 30 days (default 7 days), but it can never exceed the vault retention duration. The retention range for the daily recovery points is currently only 7 days, so it has to be raised to 90 days (three months) first, and only then can the Instant Restore retention be raised to the 14 days the application team needs for fast restores. Lengthening the retention range also applies retroactively, so the recovery points already stored in the vault keep the longer retention instead of being pruned.

perChoice.b: While the retention range for the daily recovery points stays at 7 days, an Instant Restore retention of 14 days is not allowed, because the Instant Restore retention duration can never exceed the vault retention duration. It also leaves the workload short of the required three months of daily recovery points.
perChoice.c: The Enhanced policy allows an Instant Restore retention of 1 to 30 days, so a value of 45 days is outside the supported range even though the daily point retention of 90 days would otherwise cover it.
perChoice.d: This combination is a valid configuration, but it does not satisfy the requirements: daily recovery points would be kept for only 14 days instead of three months, and fast restores would remain available for only the 7 days that are already configured.

body.stem: You have a Recovery Services vault that protects a production virtual machine with an Azure Virtual Machine backup policy. The compliance team now limits how long the platform team may keep this workload's recovery points to 90 days, and the points already stored in the vault that are older than that limit must no longer be retained. The workload must continue to be backed up every day. You need to update the backup policy in the vault. Which change should you make?

rows: Oldest recovery point stored in the vault

options.text: Reduce the retention for daily recovery points to 90 days
Set the Instant Restore retention to 90 days and leave the 180-day retention for daily recovery points unchanged
Change the backup frequency from Daily to Weekly and keep the 180-day retention
Enable Long Term Retention for monthly recovery points and keep the daily retention at 180 days

explanation.correct: A retention change is applied retroactively to the recovery points that are already stored. Lowering the retention for daily recovery points from 180 days to 90 days therefore cleans up the points that are older than 90 days, while the schedule stays at Daily so the workload is still backed up every day.

perChoice.b: Instant Restore retention controls how long the zone-redundant snapshot copies that support fast restores are kept; it does not determine how long the recovery points stored in the vault are kept. With the daily retention left at 180 days, the points older than 90 days would remain in the vault.
perChoice.c: Switching the schedule from daily to weekly removes the existing daily recovery points, including the ones that are still inside the allowed 90-day window, and it stops the daily backup runs that this workload still requires.
perChoice.d: Long Term Retention governs the monthly and yearly backup points. It does not cap the daily points, so the daily recovery points older than 90 days would still be kept in the vault.

body.stem: You have a Recovery Services vault that protects a production Linux virtual machine named app-prod-01 with an Azure Virtual Machine backup policy. The policy takes one backup every day at 02:00 and keeps recovery points for 180 days, and the vault already holds a series of daily recovery points for that machine. The workload owner has decided that a single backup each week is enough and asks you to switch the policy to a weekly schedule. You need to modify the backup policy in the vault and report to the owner what happens to the recovery points that are already stored. Which option correctly describes the result of saving this change?

rows: Backup frequency: Daily to Weekly (retention range unchanged)

options.text: The daily recovery points already stored in the vault are cleaned up when the policy is changed to a weekly frequency.
The daily recovery points already stored in the vault are kept until they expire under the current retention range when the policy is changed to a weekly frequency.
The daily recovery points already stored in the vault are moved into long-term retention when the policy is changed to a weekly frequency.
The daily recovery points already stored in the vault are converted into weekly recovery points when the policy is changed to a weekly frequency.

explanation.correct: Switching the backup frequency of an Azure Virtual Machine policy from daily to weekly cleans up the daily recovery points that are already stored in the vault. They are not carried over to the new schedule, so the VM can no longer be restored to any of those earlier daily dates, and after the change only the new weekly runs create recovery points. This is a destructive consequence the owner must be told about before the policy is saved.

perChoice.b: Letting the stored points age out under the current retention range is the behavior that applies when only the schedule days or tags change while the retention range stays the same, and when a policy moves from weekly to daily. A move from daily to weekly instead cleans up the existing daily recovery points rather than letting them expire gradually.
perChoice.c: Long Term Retention is the concept used for monthly and yearly recovery points. Changing the backup frequency does not move the stored daily recovery points into long-term retention; they are cleaned up when the schedule moves from daily to weekly.
perChoice.d: Azure Backup never converts existing daily recovery points into weekly ones. After the frequency change, the vault holds only the recovery points that the new weekly runs create, so the earlier daily dates are lost.

body.stem: You have a Recovery Services vault named rsvault-prod that protects several Azure virtual machines with the Azure Virtual Machine policies listed below. The business wants app-vm-01 protected every 6 hours with recovery points kept for 30 days, while every other virtual machine in the vault must keep the schedule and retention it runs today. You need to change the backup policy applied to app-vm-01 only. Which option should you take?

options.text: Create an Azure Virtual Machine policy with an hourly interval of 6 hours and a retention of 30 days, then assign it to app-vm-01 from the vault item dashboard and choose Save, which applies the schedule immediately.

Open the HourlyBackup policy with Modify, change its hourly interval to 6 hours and its retention to 30 days, and save it, which applies the schedule immediately to app-vm-01 and to the other virtual machines assigned to HourlyBackup.
Assign the existing NightlyCore Azure Virtual Machine policy to app-vm-01 from the vault item dashboard and then choose Save, which applies the schedule immediately to that machine.
Run Backup Now for app-vm-01 and set Retain Backup Till to 30 days to create an extra recovery point with the required retention, which applies the schedule immediately to that machine.

explanation.correct: app-vm-01 currently shares the HourlyBackup policy with app-vm-03 and app-vm-07, so changing that policy in place would alter the schedule and retention of machines that must stay as they are. The right move is to set up a separate Azure Virtual Machine policy carrying the hourly 6-hour interval and the 30-day retention, then assign it to app-vm-01 from the vault item dashboard and select Save, which applies the assignment immediately to that machine only.

perChoice.b: Modify edits the existing policy itself, so every virtual machine assigned to HourlyBackup (app-vm-01, app-vm-03 and app-vm-07) would start running the 6-hour interval with 30-day retention. That violates the requirement that the other machines keep their current schedule and retention.
perChoice.c: The NightlyCore policy is a daily policy that runs at 02:00, so assigning it to app-vm-01 would produce one backup per day rather than one every 6 hours. Its 30-day retention matches the requirement, but its frequency does not, and the change would still not deliver the required 6-hour schedule.
perChoice.d: Backup Now runs an extra on-demand job and the Retain Backup Till field sets the retention of that single on-demand recovery point only. Neither of them changes the schedule or the retention of the policy assigned to app-vm-01, so the machine would keep running every 4 hours with 90-day retention.

body.stem: You have a Recovery Services vault named rsvault-prod that protects a group of Azure virtual machines with an Enhanced Azure Virtual Machine backup policy called CorpPolicy. The audit team now requires the policy to produce a recovery point on a specific day of every month that is kept for seven years and a recovery point on a specific day of every year that is kept for ten years, in addition to the daily points the policy produces today. You need to update the backup policy in the vault so that both requirements are met. Which change should you make?

options.text: Add a monthly retention rule that runs on a chosen day of the month with a retention range of 84 months, and a yearly retention rule that runs on a chosen day of the year with a retention range of 10 years, keeping the daily schedule and its 180-day retention as they are.

Add a monthly retention rule that runs on a chosen day of the month with a retention range of 60 months, and a yearly retention rule that runs on a chosen day of the year with a retention range of 10 years, keeping the daily schedule and its 180-day retention as they are.

Add a monthly retention rule that runs on a chosen day of the month with a retention range of 84 months, and a yearly retention rule that runs on a chosen day of the year with a retention range of 5 years, keeping the daily schedule and its 180-day retention as they are.
Extend the daily retention range to 2,555 days and add a yearly retention rule that runs on a chosen day of the year with a retention range of 10 years, without adding a monthly rule.

explanation.correct: Retention can be defined separately for daily, weekly, monthly and yearly backup points, and the monthly and yearly ones are the long-term retention rules: a monthly rule fires on a chosen day of the month and a yearly rule on a chosen day of the year. Both ranges are editable, and their defaults are 60 months for monthly points and 10 years for yearly points. Seven years of monthly points therefore needs the monthly rule set to 84 months, and the ten-year audit requirement is met by a yearly rule of 10 years, while the daily schedule and its 180-day retention stay untouched so the daily points the policy produces today are unaffected.

perChoice.b: 60 months is only five years - it is the default for monthly points - so the monthly points would be cleaned up after five years instead of the required seven. The yearly rule in this option is right, but the monthly rule is not.
perChoice.c: The monthly rule of 84 months satisfies the seven-year requirement, but the yearly rule of 5 years keeps the yearly point for only half of the ten years the audit team asked for.
perChoice.d: Lengthening the daily retention range only changes how long the daily points are kept; it adds no rule that fires on a chosen day of the month, so the monthly requirement is not met. It would also store every daily point for seven years, which increases vault storage cost.

body.stem: You have a Recovery Services vault named rsvault-westus that protects a Windows virtual machine named svc-vm-14 with the Azure Virtual Machine backup policy shown below. The business wants the per-snapshot cost for this virtual machine lowered, the read-only reference data that is mounted by eight other virtual machines and the scratch logs that are regenerated every hour left out of the recovery points produced from now on, and the customer and order records on Data disk 1 still protected. You need to update how this workload is backed up in the vault. Which change should you make?

options.text: Enable selective disk backup for the Azure Virtual Machine backup policy and deselect Data disk 2 and Data disk 3
Enable selective disk backup for the Azure Virtual Machine backup policy in the MARS console so that Data disk 2 and Data disk 3 are skipped
Raise the Instant Restore snapshot retention of the Azure Virtual Machine backup policy to 30 days and set the daily retention range to 30 days
Keep the Azure Virtual Machine backup policy as it is and detach Data disk 2 and Data disk 3 from the virtual machine before every scheduled backup, reattaching them when the job ends

explanation.correct: Selective disk backup is the documented way to protect only a subset of the data disks attached to a virtual machine: noncritical or shared disks are left out of the backup, the snapshot cost is cut, and each recovery point then contains only the included disks, which can be restored from Instant Restore or from the vault tier. Turning it on for the Azure Virtual Machine backup policy and deselecting Data disk 2 (the read-only data mounted by eight other virtual machines) and Data disk 3 (the hourly scratch logs) leaves Data disk 1 with the customer and order records, along with the OS disk, as the protected content of every new recovery point.

perChoice.b: The file and folder settings for the MARS agent are specified in the MARS console, and the MARS agent covers files, folders and system state on on-premises Windows servers and on Azure VMs. It has no knowledge of which disks are attached to an Azure virtual machine, so a MARS configuration cannot decide which of those disks are written into the recovery points of svc-vm-14.
perChoice.c: Extending the Instant Restore snapshot retention only keeps more snapshots in the snapshot tier and adds to the cost of the policy; it removes nothing from the recovery points. Data disk 2 and Data disk 3 would still be captured in every backup, so the snapshot cost would not fall.
perChoice.d: The backup service does not detach or reattach data disks for you, and taking the shared reference data and the scratch disk offline around every job would disrupt the workload that reads them and still require manual work each night. The disks stay attached and are kept out of the recovery points by the backup configuration itself.

body.stem: You have a Recovery Services vault that protects an Azure Linux virtual machine with an Azure Virtual Machine backup policy. The platform team wants the snapshot copies that support a fast restore to remain available for the whole period that the vault holds recovery points, and the workload owner accepts that the platform could lose up to half a day of changes if it fails. The policy runs on the schedule shown in the exhibit. You need to update the backup policy so that both requirements are met. Which change should you make?

exhibit.text:
Backup policy            : CorpPolicy
Policy subtype           : Enhanced
Backup frequency         : Hourly
Start time               : 08:00
Repeat every             : 4 hours
Duration                 : 24 hours
Instant Restore retention: 7 days
Recovery point retention in the vault : 30 days

options.text: Keep the backup frequency on Hourly, set the repeat interval to 4 hours, and set Instant Restore retention to 30 days.
Keep the backup frequency on Hourly, set the repeat interval to 6 hours, and set Instant Restore retention to 30 days.
Keep the backup frequency on Hourly, set the repeat interval to 12 hours, and set Instant Restore retention to 30 days.
Keep the backup frequency on Hourly, set the repeat interval to 24 hours, and set Instant Restore retention to 30 days.

explanation.correct: The hourly frequency can use a repeat interval of 4, 6, 8, 12 or 24 hours, and the recovery point objective on an hourly schedule ranges from a 4-hour floor to a 24-hour ceiling. The workload owner tolerates at most half a day of loss, so the 24-hour interval is out. The number of snapshots taken per day also caps the allowed Instant Restore retention: every 4 hours over a 24-hour duration means six scheduled snapshots, and the more snapshots per day, the fewer days of retention are permitted. That rules out the 4-hour and 6-hour intervals when the requirement is the full 30 days the vault holds recovery points. The 12-hour interval is the one that lets snapshot retention rise to 30 days, and 30 days is both the maximum Instant Restore retention and equal to the vault's retention duration, which it can never exceed.

perChoice.a: Six scheduled snapshots a day (every 4 hours across the 24-hour duration) reduce the maximum allowed Instant Restore retention below the full 30 days the vault keeps its recovery points, so the required window is not delivered even though the recovery point objective is the tightest of the four.
perChoice.b: A 6-hour interval still schedules four snapshots a day, more than the 12-hour interval, so the maximum allowed Instant Restore retention stays below 30 days and the requirement for the whole vault retention period is not met.
perChoice.d: A 24-hour repeat interval pushes the recovery point objective to the 24-hour ceiling, which exceeds the half-day loss the workload owner accepts, even though it produces the fewest snapshots and therefore the most generous retention allowance.

body.stem: You have a Recovery Services vault named rsvault-prod that protects a group of Azure Linux virtual machines with an Azure Virtual Machine backup policy called CorpPolicy. The exhibit shows how this workload is protected today. The business has approved five changes to how this workload is protected, and you need every one of them to take effect in the vault. Which single setting or action satisfies each approved requirement? Match each requirement to the setting or action you would use.

rows: Time each recovery point is kept in the vault
Time a snapshot copy that supports a fast recovery is kept
Storage used for the snapshot copies

items.text: Backup frequency
Instant Restore retention
Retention range
Policy subtype
Backup Now
Selective disk backup

slots.label: The snapshot copies that support a fast recovery must survive the failure of a single availability zone.
Each snapshot copy that supports a fast recovery must remain available for a fortnight after the capture it belongs to.
No recovery point that is more than one year old may be kept in the vault.
The workload must be captured every six hours so that no more than six hours of work is lost when a machine fails.
The operations team wants two extra captures of each machine every day, triggered by hand at times they choose, with each of those captures kept until a date they name.

explanation.correct: Each requirement is satisfied by exactly one setting or action on the policy: the goal of surviving a single availability zone failure is met by moving to the Enhanced policy subtype, whose snapshot storage is zone-redundant; the fourteen-day life of the fast-recovery snapshot copies is set with the Instant Restore retention value (1 to 30 days, 7 days by default) and stays well under the vault retention duration; the point at which recovery points are dropped from the vault is governed by the retention range, which the exhibit shows as 180 days today and which can be set to 365 days; a repeating capture every six hours comes from the schedule frequency, where Hourly can repeat at 4, 6, 8, 12 or 24 hours across a 24-hour duration; and two hand-started extra captures with an operator-chosen end date are produced with the on-demand Backup Now action and its Retain Backup Till field. Selective disk backup belongs in no slot because it only leaves disks out of a capture and none of the five requirements asks for that.

perChoice.freq: Backup frequency is where the repeating schedule is configured, with Hourly, Daily and Weekly choices; setting it to Hourly repeating every 6 hours over a 24-hour duration produces the required capture every six hours. The zone-resilience goal is met by the subtype instead, and the hand-started extra captures are an on-demand action rather than a schedule.
perChoice.instr: Instant Restore retention controls how long each recovery snapshot stays available for a fast recovery; 14 days is inside the 1 to 30 day range, is longer than the 7 days in the exhibit, and does not exceed the duration for which points are kept in the vault.
perChoice.range: The retention range decides how long recovery points are kept in the vault; setting it to 365 days satisfies the one-year limit, and the value that is saved is imposed on the points already stored, so any point beyond that age is removed.
perChoice.subtype: Only the Enhanced subtype stores the Instant Restore snapshots redundantly across availability zones, so this requirement is met by changing the policy subtype; remember that a VM once protected with the Enhanced subtype cannot be moved back to Standard.
perChoice.now: Backup Now is the on-demand action: the operator triggers each extra capture by hand and names the date up to which that copy is kept in the Retain Backup Till field. It produces copies outside the scheduled run and does not alter the schedule itself.
perChoice.selective: Selective disk backup excludes disks from the recovery points to reduce snapshot cost, and none of the five requirements asks for any disk to be left out, so it fits no slot.

body.stem: You have two Recovery Services vaults in the East US region: one that already protects workloads which are being retired, and one that is being prepared for a new workload. The exhibit shows their current settings. You need to onboard app-vm-21, decide how its recovery points are stored, and wind down the two retired virtual machines. Which option should you use for each requirement?

rows: Region: East US. Redundancy: GRS (the default). No workload is protected by it yet.
Policy CorpPolicy: subtype Standard, schedule daily at 02:00, recovery points kept for 180 days.
Protected by CorpPolicy in rsvault-prod. Scheduled runs finish successfully. The workload is being retired.
Protected by CorpPolicy in rsvault-prod. Scheduled runs finish successfully. The workload is being retired.
Not yet protected. Uses a Trusted Launch image. One Ultra Disk and one Premium SSD v2 data disk attached.

items.text: Create a new Azure Virtual Machine backup policy with the Enhanced subtype
Set the vault redundancy to ZRS
Set the backup schedule frequency to Hourly with a 6-hour repeat interval
Stop protection and retain backup data
Stop protection and delete backup data
Set the vault redundancy to LRS
Create a new Azure Virtual Machine backup policy with the Standard subtype
Set the backup schedule frequency to Daily

slots.label: app-vm-21 must be covered several times a day, and its Trusted Launch image and Ultra Disk must be supported
app-vm-21 must receive exactly four recovery points each day
Everything stored for app-vm-21 must survive the loss of an availability zone in East US without being copied to another region
app-vm-07 is being retired: no further scheduled runs, its stored recovery points stay restorable, and scheduled runs can start again later
app-vm-08 is being retired and the business has decided that restoring this workload must no longer be possible

explanation.correct: app-vm-21 is not yet protected and must be covered several times a day with support for its Trusted Launch image, Ultra Disk and Premium SSD v2, so it needs a new policy with the Enhanced subtype, with an Hourly schedule repeating every 6 hours to yield four recovery points each day. Its recovery points must survive an availability-zone failure in East US without leaving that region, which is what ZRS provides (the vault's current GRS setting instead replicates to a paired secondary region). app-vm-07 must keep its stored recovery points restorable with the ability to resume runs later, which is 'Stop protection and retain backup data'. app-vm-08 must no longer be restorable, which is 'Stop protection and delete backup data'.

perChoice.i1: app-vm-21 uses a Trusted Launch image and has Ultra Disk and Premium SSD v2 data disks, and it must be covered several times a day. Standard cannot protect Ultra Disk or Premium SSD v2 and does not offer multiple backups per day, while Enhanced supports both; because app-vm-21 is not yet protected, a new policy with the Enhanced subtype applies it.
perChoice.i2: ZRS keeps the stored recovery points across availability zones while keeping them in the same region, so an availability-zone failure in East US does not lose them and they never leave that region. GRS, the vault's current setting, instead replicates to a paired secondary region.
perChoice.i3: An hourly schedule repeating every 6 hours produces four recovery points across the day, which matches the coverage requested for app-vm-21. Hourly intervals of 4, 6, 8, 12 or 24 hours can be chosen, and the 4-hour interval would give six points a day instead.
perChoice.i4: This action halts future scheduled runs while keeping the stored recovery points, so app-vm-07's recovery points remain restorable and protection can be started again later, because Resume backup stays available.
perChoice.i5: This action halts future scheduled runs and wipes the stored recovery points, so restoring app-vm-08 is no longer possible and Resume backup is not offered; the data is kept in a soft-delete state for 14 days.
perChoice.i6: LRS keeps three copies in a single datacenter, which protects against rack or drive failure but not against the loss of an availability zone, so it does not meet the zone-resilience requirement.
perChoice.i7: Standard is the cheaper, established behavior, but it cannot protect Ultra Disk or Premium SSD v2 and it does not provide several backups per day, so it does not meet the requirements for app-vm-21.
perChoice.i8: A daily schedule produces a single recovery point each day, so it cannot deliver the four points a day that app-vm-21 needs; only an hourly schedule with a 6-hour repeat interval gives four.

body.stem: You have a Recovery Services vault named rsvault-prod that protects 14 Azure virtual machines with an hourly backup policy and also stores file and folder data for one on-premises Windows server. The exhibit shows the current environment state plus the requests raised by the operations, security, and finance teams. Every request has to be met. Match each request to the setting or action that satisfies it.

rows: 14 virtual machines covered by one hourly backup policy
One Windows Server 2019 whose files and folders are already captured; one Linux application server that the team wants included
A single administrator holds Contributor rights on the vault and performs the critical changes
The oldest ones sit in the cheapest storage available in the vault

items.text: Deploy DPM or MABS for the on-premises machine
Install the MARS agent on the on-premises machine
Enable Multi-User Authorization in the vault
Assign an Azure RBAC role in the vault for backup administration
Move the recovery points from the Archive tier to the Vault-Standard tier
Move the recovery points from the Vault-Standard tier to the Archive tier
Set the Retain Backup Till value in the Backup Now blade of the Azure portal
Set the Instant Restore retention to 45 days

slots.label: The on-premises Linux application server in the company datacenter must be brought into this vault, and the team cannot change the operating system it runs
The security team wants an extra confirmation step before the most sensitive changes to the data held in this vault are carried out
The restore team wants the oldest stored copies in this vault, which sit in the cheapest storage, to be brought back faster
When the operators trigger an immediate job for a virtual machine, they must be able to state how long that job should be kept

explanation.correct: The four requests are met by four different capabilities: an on-premises Linux machine has to be brought in through DPM or MABS because the agent used for on-premises Windows servers has no Linux support; Multi-User Authorization puts an Azure Resource Guard approval layer in front of critical vault operations; recovery points can be moved out of the Archive tier into the Vault-Standard tier, which gives faster access at a higher storage cost; and the Retain Backup Till field in the Backup Now pane is what decides how long an on-demand backup is kept.

perChoice.i1: The MARS agent covers on-premises Windows machines only, so a Linux server in the datacenter has to be brought in through a DPM or MABS server, which then backs it up to the vault.
perChoice.i2: The MARS agent runs on on-premises Windows machines for files, folders, and system state; it has no Linux support, so it cannot cover the Linux application server.
perChoice.i3: Multi-User Authorization adds an Azure Resource Guard layer, so critical operations in the vault need an additional confirmation before they run.
perChoice.i4: An Azure RBAC role assignment decides who may act on the vault, but it does not add the extra confirmation step for critical operations that Multi-User Authorization provides.
perChoice.i5: Recovery points can be moved from the Archive tier to the Vault-Standard tier for restore or management work, and the Vault-Standard tier offers faster access at a higher storage cost, which is exactly what the restore team asked for.
perChoice.i6: This moves the data in the opposite direction, into the cheapest and slowest storage; the request was for faster access to the oldest stored copies.
perChoice.i7: In the Backup Now pane the Retain Backup Till field holds the date until which the on-demand backup is kept, so it is the control that lets the operators state how long an immediate job is retained.
perChoice.i8: The Instant Restore retention controls how long the snapshots used for a fast restore are kept; it does not decide the retention of an on-demand job, which comes from the value entered when the job is triggered.

body.stem: You have a new platform team standing up Azure Backup for the workloads listed in the exhibit. The three new Azure virtual machines each get their own new Recovery Services vault, while hotline-vm-09 stays on the policy it already has. You need to pick the Azure Backup setting, component or field that meets each business requirement. Which option should you use for each requirement? Match each requirement to the option you would use.

exhibit.text:
Workload        | Where it runs                                                          | Current protection
payments-vm-01  | Azure virtual machine in East US                                        | Not protected yet
wiki-vm-02      | Azure virtual machine in West Europe; the region has three availability zones | Not protected yet
test-vm-03      | Azure virtual machine in East US; hosted in a single datacenter           | Not protected yet
filesrv-01      | On-premises Windows Server in the corporate datacenter                    | One shared folder and the system state
hotline-vm-09   | Azure virtual machine with an existing policy                            | Daily recovery points, kept for 7 days

items.text: LRS
GRS
ZRS
Multi-User Authorization
MARS agent
Retain Backup Till
VMSnapshot extension

slots.label: Recovery points for payments-vm-01 must still be restorable after the whole East US region is lost
Recovery points for wiki-vm-02 must survive the loss of one availability zone in West Europe, and no copy may be stored outside that region
Recovery points for test-vm-03 only need to survive a single rack or drive failure, because the sandbox can be rebuilt if the whole region is gone
Critical operations on any vault that the team manages must not run without a second approval from the platform owner
The shared folder on filesrv-01 must be protected in a Recovery Services vault together with the Azure workloads
The recovery point taken by hand after the hotline-vm-09 outage must be kept for 30 days even though the policy keeps daily points for only 7 days

explanation.correct: Each requirement maps to one Azure Backup option. A whole-region outage is covered by GRS, which keeps a copy in a paired secondary region. Surviving the loss of one availability zone while every copy stays in the same region calls for ZRS. Tolerating only a rack or drive failure calls for LRS, which replicates three times inside one datacenter. Requiring a second approval before critical vault operations run calls for Multi-User Authorization, which layers Azure Resource Guard over the vault. Protecting an on-premises Windows server's shared folder in a Recovery Services vault calls for the MARS agent. Deciding how long a hand-triggered recovery point is kept calls for the Retain Backup Till field. The VMSnapshot extension is installed by the Azure VM agent on Azure virtual machines and meets none of these requirements.

perChoice.i1: LRS replicates data three times within a single datacenter, so it covers server rack and drive failures only. It offers nothing against the loss of an availability zone or of a whole region, which is exactly the tolerance the sandbox workload accepts.
perChoice.i2: GRS replicates data to a secondary region, so recovery points stay restorable after a region-wide outage. It does not satisfy the requirement that no copy be stored outside the current region, and it is more than the sandbox workload needs.
perChoice.i3: ZRS replicates data across availability zones and guarantees data residency in the same region, which matches the zone-loss requirement. It does not protect against the complete loss of the region.
perChoice.i4: Multi-User Authorization adds an Azure Resource Guard layer so that critical operations need a second approval. It changes no schedule, no retention and no storage location for recovery points.
perChoice.i5: The MARS agent runs on on-premises Windows servers and backs up files, folders and the system state into a Recovery Services vault. It is not the component that protects an Azure virtual machine.
perChoice.i6: The Retain Backup Till field in the Backup Now pane sets how long that on-demand recovery point is kept, which is what the 30-day requirement needs. It does not change the policy schedule or the policy's own retention.
perChoice.i7: The VMSnapshot extension is installed by the Azure VM agent on Windows virtual machines in Azure to coordinate their snapshots. It does not apply to an on-premises server, to where recovery points are stored, to approval workflows or to how long an on-demand point is kept.

body.stem: You are the Azure administrator responsible for backup policy for a platform team. A Recovery Services vault named rsvault-prod in the East US region protects three Azure virtual machines and holds their recovery points, one on-premises Windows server on the corporate network is not yet protected, and two other teams each want their own new vault in East US. The exhibit lists the objects involved. Six candidate settings, components, or actions are on the table, and each approved request below has to be satisfied. Match every approved request to the setting, component, or action that delivers it.

exhibit.text:
Object            | Current state
------------------|-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Vault rsvault-prod | East US; protects app-vm-01, app-vm-02 and app-vm-03
app-vm-03         | Its contract ends this month and the team wants it retired
fileserver-02     | On-premises Windows server on the corporate network; not yet protected
team-orders       | New team; expects its own vault in East US
team-billing      | New team; expects its own vault in East US

items.text: Create the vault with GRS redundancy
Create the vault with ZRS redundancy
Enable Multi-User Authorization on the vault
Install and configure the MARS agent on the on-premises Windows server
Stop protection and retain backup data for the retired virtual machine
Create the vault with LRS redundancy

slots.label: team-orders: the recovery points of its new vault must be usable even if the whole East US region is lost, so copies of them have to be kept in another region
team-billing: the recovery points of its new vault must stay inside East US and survive the loss of one availability zone
Actions on rsvault-prod that the platform classifies as critical must not be carried out by one person alone; a second approver has to sign off first
The shared document share on fileserver-02 must be captured into rsvault-prod
app-vm-03 must no longer produce scheduled jobs, while the recovery points already in rsvault-prod stay available for restore and remain billable

explanation.correct: team-orders needs its recovery points to survive the loss of the whole East US region, so its new vault is created with GRS redundancy, which replicates the data to a secondary region and is the default for Recovery Services vaults. team-billing needs the recovery points to stay in East US yet survive the failure of one availability zone, so its vault is created with ZRS redundancy, which spreads the data across availability zones in the same region. The critical vault actions on rsvault-prod must not be run by one person alone, so Multi-User Authorization is enabled on the vault, adding the Azure Resource Guard layer that requires a second administrator's approval. The shared document share on the on-premises Windows server fileserver-02 is protected by installing and configuring the MARS agent, which is the agent used for files and folders on on-premises Windows servers (the VM backup extension only applies to Azure VMs). Finally, app-vm-03 must end its scheduled jobs while keeping the recovery points already stored, restorable and still charged for, which is exactly the 'Stop protection and retain backup data' behaviour; the delete variant would remove the recovery points and make restore impossible. The LRS option matches neither vault request: it keeps three copies in a single datacenter and only covers rack or drive failures.

perChoice.a: Correct for the team-orders request. GRS replicates the vault's data to a secondary region and is used to protect against region-wide outages, which is what a workload needing usable recovery points after the loss of East US requires.
perChoice.b: Correct for the team-billing request. ZRS replicates the data across availability zones while guaranteeing data residency in the same region, so the recovery points stay in East US and survive the loss of a single zone.
perChoice.c: Correct for the critical-operations request. Multi-User Authorization adds an Azure Resource Guard layer to the vault so that operations on critical data are approved by a second administrator before they can run.
perChoice.d: Correct for the fileserver-02 request. The MARS agent runs on on-premises Windows servers to back up files and folders, so it is the component that captures the shared document share into the vault; the Azure VM backup extension is only installed on Azure virtual machines.
perChoice.e: Correct for the app-vm-03 request. This option stops all future backup jobs but keeps the recovery points that have already been backed up; the recovery points remain restorable, keep incurring charges while they sit in the vault, and protection can be resumed later.
perChoice.f: Fits no request. LRS replicates the data three times inside a single datacenter in the primary region and only protects against server rack and drive failures; it neither survives the loss of a zone nor keeps a copy in another region, so it satisfies neither vault request.

body.stem: You are standing up Azure Backup for a new platform in the East US region. The platform has three virtual machines to protect, and no Recovery Services vault exists for it yet, so you must create the vault and then author a new Azure Virtual Machine backup policy inside it. The exhibit lists the environment and the objectives the business has approved, and each objective has to be delivered by a single setting or choice. Which setting or choice should you use for each objective? Match each objective to the setting or choice you would use.

rows: Recovery Services vault for the platform
Windows, Trusted Launch image, one Premium SSD v2 data disk
Windows, Trusted Launch image, one Ultra Disk data disk
Rebuildable from configuration management and upstream data feeds, so the vault is not the system of record

items.text: Hourly
ZRS
Enhanced
Daily
LRS
Long Term Retention (LTR)
GRS
Standard

slots.label: Keep the protected workload recoverable if the entire East US region becomes unavailable
Keep the vault's stored data inside East US while still surviving the loss of one availability zone
Accept the loss of the vault's stored data if the datacenter that holds it fails, because the platform can rebuild its own data
Protect the Trusted Launch virtual machines and their Premium SSD v2 and Ultra Disk data disks, and take more than one backup each day
Take a backup every four hours for the protected virtual machines
Keep a point taken on a chosen day of every month for five years and a point taken on a chosen day of every year for ten years

explanation.correct: Each objective maps to one setting. Zone-redundant multi-daily coverage that also covers Trusted Launch virtual machines and Ultra Disk or Premium SSD v2 data disks comes from the Enhanced policy subtype. A repeating cycle through the day, with a backup every four hours, is the Hourly schedule frequency. Points chosen for a specific day of the month and for a specific day of the year are held under Long Term Retention. The vault redundancy choice decides which outage the workload survives: GRS keeps a copy in a paired secondary region so a regional outage is survivable, ZRS keeps the data in the deployment region while surviving an availability zone outage, and LRS keeps three copies in a single datacenter, which is acceptable here only because the platform's data is rebuildable.

perChoice.i1: This schedule frequency produces repeated backups through the day, so it is the choice that delivers the objective calling for a backup every four hours.
perChoice.i2: Storing the vault's data in availability zones keeps it inside the deployment region while still surviving the loss of a zone, which is exactly what that objective asks for.
perChoice.i3: This policy subtype allows more than one backup per day and covers Trusted Launch virtual machines and Ultra Disk or Premium SSD v2 data disks, so it satisfies the objective about those workloads.
perChoice.i4: A once-per-day schedule does not produce the repeated backups every four hours that the corresponding objective requires, so it belongs to no objective here.
perChoice.i5: Keeping three copies in a single datacenter matches the objective that accepts datacenter-level loss, because the platform's data can be rebuilt and the vault is not the system of record.
perChoice.i6: Monthly and yearly recovery points fall under Long Term Retention, which is where a point chosen for every month and a point chosen for every year are stored, so this item serves that objective.
perChoice.i7: Replication into a paired secondary region keeps the workload recoverable when the deployment region itself is lost, which is the objective it satisfies.
perChoice.i8: This policy subtype suits a workload that needs one backup per day on supported disk types, but it cannot protect Ultra Disk or Premium SSD v2 data disks and does not offer multi-daily coverage, so it fits no objective in this scenario.

body.stem: You have a Recovery Services vault named rsvault-prod that protects six Azure virtual machines with a single Azure Virtual Machine backup policy. Two of those machines, app-vm-31 and app-vm-32, are being switched off and removed, and the exhibit shows what is stored for each of them along with the request raised by the owner of each workload. Neither of the two workloads should keep running its scheduled backups once the machine is gone, and the other four protected machines must stay exactly as they are today. You need to wind down the two workloads and also tell the platform team for how long the erased data of app-vm-32 can still be recovered. Which action should you take for each workload, and which value answers the platform team's question?

exhibit.text:
Item          | Current state                                                                                 | Request raised
--------------|----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
rsvault-prod  | East US; six Azure virtual machines protected by one Azure Virtual Machine policy that runs daily | The four machines that are not being retired must keep the schedule they run today and the recovery points they hold today
app-vm-31     | Daily recovery points stored in the vault for the last 180 days; machine switched off and removed  | The team must still be able to restore the machine from one of the recovery points already held in the vault, and the scheduled backups must be able to start again if the machine ever comes back
app-vm-32     | Daily recovery points stored in the vault for the last 180 days; machine switched off and removed  | The stored recovery points must be erased so that nobody can restore the workload, and the platform team wants to know for how long a technical recovery of the erased data stays possible

body.statement: For app-vm-31, {{vm31Action}}. For app-vm-32, {{vm32Action}}. The erased data of app-vm-32 can still be recovered for {{eraseWindow}}.

options.text: Stop protection and retain backup data
Stop protection and delete backup data
Delete backup data from the vault item dashboard
Resume backup
Stop protection and retain backup data
Stop protection and delete backup data
Delete backup data from the vault item dashboard
Resume backup
7 days
14 days
30 days
90 days

explanation.correct: app-vm-31 is being removed but its owner still needs a rollback path and the ability to start the backups again later, so the right action is to stop its protection while keeping the recovery points in the vault: future backup jobs stop, the points stay available for a restore, storage is still billed, and the Resume backup option remains offered. app-vm-32 must have its stored points erased, so the right action is to stop its protection and delete the backup data, which halts the jobs, removes all recovery points, blocks any restore and removes the Resume backup option; the backed-up data is then held for 14 days in a soft-deleted state, which is the window in which the erased data can still be recovered.

perChoice.vm31Action:b: This wipes the recovery points that app-vm-31 needs for a rollback, so the workload could no longer be restored and the possibility of starting its backups again would disappear as well.
perChoice.vm31Action:c: This control is only enabled once protection has already been stopped while keeping the data, and it removes every recovery point at once, so it cannot deliver the restore capability the owner asked for on its own.
perChoice.vm31Action:d: This re-arms the schedule for a machine that is being removed; it does not end anything, so the workload would still be reported as protected and its backup item would keep accruing charges.
perChoice.vm32Action:a: This keeps the recovery points in the vault and leaves the workload restorable, which is the opposite of what the owner of app-vm-32 asked for.
perChoice.vm32Action:c: This control becomes available only when protection was previously stopped while keeping the data; it removes all recovery points but does not perform the stop step itself, so it does not cover the whole request for this workload.
perChoice.vm32Action:d: This starts the schedule again rather than ending it, and it is not offered once the stored data has been erased.
perChoice.eraseWindow:a: After the stored data is erased it is held for 14 days in a soft-deleted state, so the window is not 7 days.
perChoice.eraseWindow:c: After the stored data is erased it is held for 14 days in a soft-deleted state, so the window is not 30 days.
perChoice.eraseWindow:d: After the stored data is erased it is held for 14 days in a soft-deleted state, so the window is not 90 days.

body.stem: You have a Recovery Services vault named rsvault-prod that protects a Linux virtual machine running an order-processing database with an Azure Virtual Machine backup policy. After the last restore of that machine, the database had to be put through crash recovery by hand and its write-ahead log replayed before the service would start. The business now wants each recovery point for this workload to be application-consistent, so that a restore brings the database up without any manual repair work. You need to change how this workload is protected in the vault. Which change should you make?

exhibit.text:
Recovery Services vault : rsvault-prod (East US)
Protected workload    : orders-vm-03 (Azure Virtual Machine)
Operating system      : Ubuntu 22.04 LTS
Backup policy name    : OrdersPolicy
Policy subtype        : Standard
Backup schedule       : Daily at 01:00
Recovery point retention : 30 days
Snapshot copies kept for fast restore : 7 days
Guest backup extension : VMSnapshotLinux
Restore result reported by operations : database required crash recovery by hand and write-ahead log replay before the service started

options.text: Configure pre-backup and post-backup scripts so the database is quiesced during the snapshot
Configure the Enhanced policy subtype so the backup captures all attached disks together during a single crash-consistent snapshot
Configure VSS integration so the guest is able to create an application-consistent snapshot of the running database
Configure the MARS agent and use the MARS console to capture the database files and folders

explanation.correct: On a Linux virtual machine, Azure Backup takes a file-consistent backup, and application-consistent recovery points are obtained only by manually customizing pre/post scripts. Adding pre-backup and post-backup scripts lets the database be quiesced (for example, flushed and frozen) around the snapshot, so the recovery point is application-consistent and the restored database starts without manual crash recovery or write-ahead log replay. That is exactly the symptom the operations team reported, so the scripts are the change that fixes it.

perChoice.change:b: This workload runs Linux, so the Enhanced subtype buys zone-redundant Instant Restore storage, shorter intervals between backups, Trusted Launch support, Premium SSD v2 and Ultra Disk support, and snapshots that capture several disks together, but those snapshots are crash-consistent. A restored database still has to be crash-recovered by hand, so the manual repair work the business wants removed remains. Enhanced is also a one-way move: a virtual machine already protected with Enhanced cannot be switched back to Standard.
perChoice.change:c: Coordinating with VSS is the Windows mechanism: for running Windows virtual machines, Azure Backup coordinates with the Volume Shadow Copy Service to take an app-consistent snapshot (full VSS backup by default, with a file-consistent fallback when an app-consistent snapshot cannot be taken). A Linux guest does not use VSS, so this setting does not apply to the machine in the scenario and would not change the consistency of its recovery points.
perChoice.change:d: The MARS agent covers files, folders and system state, and its file/folder settings are configured in the MARS console rather than in the Azure Virtual Machine backup policy. Because it does not use application VSS writers, it does not capture app-consistent snapshots, so switching this workload to the MARS agent would still leave the database needing crash recovery after a restore. On-premises Linux machines also cannot be backed up directly with the MARS agent.

body.stem: You have a Recovery Services vault named rsvault-prod that protects a group of Azure virtual machines with an Azure Virtual Machine backup policy called CorpPolicy, whose daily recovery points are kept for 90 days to satisfy a compliance limit. Two new requests have come in for this vault. The platform team wants an additional policy for a batch of newer virtual machines, and the exhibit lists what that policy has to deliver. The owner of app-vm-12 also wants one extra recovery point captured by hand today, before a risky change to that machine, and that point must still be available in three years even though CorpPolicy's own retention ends much sooner. You need to deliver both requests inside the vault. Which setting or action should you use for each request?

rows: Policy subtype for the new policy
Enhanced — the batch includes virtual machines created from Trusted Launch images
Two backup runs during every day
Start time of the first run
Captured by hand today; must remain available for three years
CorpPolicy — one run each day at 02:00; daily points kept for 90 days

body.statement: To deliver the request for the new policy you should {{policySchedule}}, and to satisfy the request for the extra recovery point for app-vm-12 you should {{extraPoint}}.

options.text: Hourly schedule with a start time of 20:00, a repeat interval of 12 hours and a duration of 24 hours
Hourly schedule with a start time of 20:00, a repeat interval of 4 hours and a duration of 24 hours
Hourly schedule with a start time of 20:00, a repeat interval of 24 hours and a duration of 24 hours
Hourly schedule with a start time of 08:00, a repeat interval of 12 hours and a duration of 24 hours
Run Backup Now and set Retain Backup Till to 3 years
Run Backup Now and set Retain Backup Till to 90 days
Wait for the next scheduled backup and set Retain Backup Till to 3 years
Change the daily retention of the policy to 3 years and leave the schedule alone

explanation.correct: Two different pieces of work are needed. For the new policy, the schedule must be Hourly, the first run has to start at 20:00, the repeat interval has to be 12 hours — the intervals that can be chosen are 4, 6, 8, 12 and 24 hours, and only 12 hours gives the two runs per day the request asks for — and the duration has to be 24 hours so the window covers the entire day. For app-vm-12, the extra point is produced with the Backup Now operation, and the Retain Backup Till field in that pane sets the retention of the on-demand backup itself: the retention range of an on-demand backup is the value you specify when you trigger it. Entering a date three years out therefore keeps that single point available long after the 90-day retention of CorpPolicy would have removed it.

perChoice.policySchedule:b: Repeating every 4 hours across a 24-hour window produces six runs per day, not the two the request calls for; 4 hours is a valid interval but the wrong one for this workload.
perChoice.policySchedule:c: A 24-hour repeat interval inside a 24-hour duration produces only one run per day, so the second daily run the request requires would never happen.
perChoice.policySchedule:d: 08:00 is the default start time for an hourly schedule, but this request states that the first run of the day starts at 20:00; the repeat interval and duration are otherwise right.
perChoice.extraPoint:b: The value entered when the on-demand backup is triggered decides how long that point survives, so 90 days would make the extra point expire together with the policy's daily points instead of lasting three years.
perChoice.extraPoint:c: Retain Backup Till is a field of the Backup Now pane; scheduled runs take their lifetime from the policy's retention range and cannot be given an individual keep-until date, so this neither produces the extra point today nor extends its life.
perChoice.extraPoint:d: Widening the policy's daily retention affects every recovery point of every machine that uses CorpPolicy, breaks the 90-day compliance limit, and still does not capture the extra point by hand today.

body.stem: You administer a Recovery Services vault named rsvault-westus in the East US region. The vault protects app-vm-07 with an Enhanced Azure Virtual Machine backup policy, and a second virtual machine, new-vm-22, was protected with that same policy earlier today. The exhibit shows the current configuration and the two items the operations team has raised. You need to answer both of them correctly. Which option should you use for each item?

exhibit.text:
Vault                         : rsvault-westus (East US)
Policy on app-vm-07, new-vm-22 : Enhanced Azure Virtual Machine backup policy
Backup schedule               : Hourly, start 04:00, repeat every 4 hours, duration 24 hours
Instant Restore retention     : 7 days
Daily retention range         : 180 days
Job history for app-vm-07     : Six runs completed successfully in one 24-hour period;
                                the vault holds one recovery point for that period
new-vm-22                     : Created today at 09:15 and protected with the same policy;
                                its 12:00 run is in progress at the time of the request
Item raised by operations     : Run an on-demand backup of new-vm-22 right now, ahead of a
                                configuration change they are about to make
Question from operations      : app-vm-07 shows six successful runs in a single day but only
                                one recovery point in the vault - why?

body.statement: The on-demand run requested for new-vm-22 results in {{onDemand}}, and the hourly runs of app-vm-07 reach the vault as follows: {{vaultRuns}}.

options.text: the whole virtual machine being transferred to the vault, because the first scheduled backup is still running
only the blocks that changed since the previous run being transferred to the vault, because the first scheduled backup has already produced the baseline
the job waiting for the first scheduled backup to finish and then transferring only the changed blocks to the vault
the job failing and being retried later, because a backup of the virtual machine is already running
every run is transferred to the vault when that run finishes
only the last backup of the day is transferred to the vault, and the first backup of the next day is transferred when that run fails
only the first backup of the day is transferred to the vault, and the remaining runs of that day are dropped
every second run is transferred to the vault, and the number of recovery points kept in the vault is halved

explanation.correct: For the on-demand run on new-vm-22, the initial backup is still pending, and when the initial backup is pending an on-demand backup creates a full copy of the virtual machine in the Recovery Services vault; only once the initial backup is complete does an on-demand run send just the changes since the previous snapshot, because every backup to Azure after the first one is incremental. For the hourly runs of app-vm-07, only the last backup of the day is transferred to the vault, and if that run fails the first backup of the next day is transferred instead. That is why six successful runs inside one 24-hour period (a 4-hour interval over a 24-hour duration produces six scheduled snapshots) leave only one recovery point in the vault.

perChoice.onDemand:b: This describes the behaviour once the initial backup has already completed, where an on-demand run transfers only the blocks that changed since the previous snapshot. new-vm-22's initial backup has not finished yet, so the requested run does not behave this way.
perChoice.onDemand:c: The job is not queued behind the pending initial backup. When the initial backup is pending, the on-demand run creates a full copy of the virtual machine in the vault rather than waiting and then sending only changed blocks.
perChoice.onDemand:d: The run does not fail because another backup is in progress; an on-demand backup can be triggered while the initial backup is pending, and in that situation it creates a full copy of the virtual machine in the vault.
perChoice.vaultRuns:a: Each scheduled run is not transferred to the vault as it completes. With an hourly schedule only the last backup of the day is transferred to the vault, so the intermediate runs do not each produce a vaulted recovery point.
perChoice.vaultRuns:c: It is not the first backup of the day that reaches the vault. The last backup of the day is the one transferred, and if that run fails the first backup of the next day is transferred instead, which is the behaviour that produces a single recovery point for a day of hourly runs.
perChoice.vaultRuns:d: The number of recovery points is not halved by transferring every second run. Only the last backup of the day is transferred to the vault, with the first backup of the next day taking over if that run fails, so a day of six hourly runs yields one vaulted recovery point.

body.stem: You have a Recovery Services vault named rsvault-prod in the East US region that protects a group of Azure Linux virtual machines. The exhibit shows the new Azure Virtual Machine backup policy that an administrator is creating for another team; the schedule frequency has already been chosen, and the business has asked for the remaining schedule values to be left exactly as the portal supplies them, because those values already match the agreed standard. You need to complete the policy. Which schedule values does the portal supply, and how many scheduled backups does the resulting policy take over a full day?

rows: Leave at the value the portal supplies
Leave at the value the portal supplies
Leave at the value the portal supplies

body.statement: The portal supplies {{scheduleDefaults}} for this schedule, and the resulting policy takes {{dailyCount}}.

options.text: Start time 8 AM, repeat every 4 hours, duration 24 hours
Start time 2 AM, repeat every 6 hours, duration 24 hours
Start time 8 AM, repeat every 12 hours, duration 12 hours
Start time 12 AM, repeat every 8 hours, duration 24 hours
Six scheduled backups over a full day
Four scheduled backups over a full day
Eight scheduled backups over a full day
Twelve scheduled backups over a full day

explanation.correct: When the backup schedule frequency is set to Hourly, the portal pre-populates the start time with 8 AM, the repeat interval with every 4 hours and the duration with 24 hours; those are the values the business asked to keep unchanged. A 24-hour duration with a 4-hour repeat interval divides into six scheduled snapshots per day, which matches the documented example of a frequency of every 4 hours over a duration of 24 hours producing six scheduled snapshots. Worth knowing alongside this: with hourly schedules only the last backup of the day is transferred into the vault, and if that transfer fails the first backup of the next day is transferred instead.

perChoice.scheduleDefaults:b: The duration of 24 hours matches, but the portal's default start time is 8 AM and its default repeat interval is 4 hours, so 2 AM and every 6 hours are not the values supplied automatically.
perChoice.scheduleDefaults:c: The start time matches, but the default repeat interval is every 4 hours and the default duration is 24 hours, so a 12-hour repeat over a 12-hour window is not what the portal supplies.
perChoice.scheduleDefaults:d: The duration matches, but the default start time is 8 AM and the default repeat interval is every 4 hours, so 12 AM and every 8 hours are not the values supplied automatically.
perChoice.dailyCount:b: Four runs would need a 6-hour repeat interval across the full day, not the 4-hour interval the portal supplies by default.
perChoice.dailyCount:c: Eight runs would need a 3-hour interval, which is not one of the intervals that can be selected for an hourly schedule (4, 6, 8, 12 or 24 hours).
perChoice.dailyCount:d: Twelve runs would need a 2-hour interval, which is not among the intervals that can be selected for an hourly schedule.

body.stem: You are the Azure administrator for a new payroll platform. The company operates only in the East US region, and two new Recovery Services vaults plus one new Azure Virtual Machine backup policy are being set up. The exhibit lists what has already been decided. The business requires that the recovery points held in the payroll vault survive the loss of an availability zone while never being copied outside the East US region, that the new policy protect the payroll workload several times a day with the tightest spacing between recovery points that the service supports, and that no single administrator be able to remove recovery points from the analytics vault unless a second administrator has approved the operation first. You need to complete the configuration so that every requirement is met. Which setting should you use for each requirement?

rows: New vault that will hold the recovery points of the payroll platform
New vault owned by the analytics team
New Azure Virtual Machine policy to be created inside rsvault-payroll
Policy subtype already chosen for PayPolicy
pay-web, pay-db and pay-batch, all Azure virtual machines

body.statement: To meet all three requirements, configure rsvault-payroll with {{vaultRedundancy}} redundancy, run PayPolicy with {{backupSchedule}}, and {{criticalOperations}} for rsvault-analytics.

options.text: LRS
GRS
ZRS
hourly backups every 4 hours
hourly backups every 6 hours
hourly backups every 12 hours
one backup each day
enable Multi-User Authorization with Azure Resource Guard
enable Multi-User Authorization with Azure Policy assignments
enable soft delete for deleted recovery points in the Azure vault
enable cross-region restore for recovery points in the Azure vault

explanation.correct: The payroll vault needs ZRS, because zone-redundant storage replicates the recovery points across availability zones and guarantees data residency and resiliency in the same region, which is exactly what the East US zone-failure requirement asks for; LRS only protects against server rack and drive failures, and GRS copies the data to a paired region, which would break the residency requirement. PayPolicy must run hourly backups every 4 hours: with the Enhanced policy subtype Azure Backup can be scheduled as often as every 4 hours, and that is the shortest interval it supports, so this is the tightest spacing that still produces several recovery points per day. The analytics vault needs Multi-User Authorization with Azure Resource Guard, which adds the approval layer in front of critical operations such as deleting recovery points so a second administrator can sign off; soft delete only keeps deleted recovery points recoverable for a while and adds no approval step, and cross-region restore only changes where a restore can be performed.

perChoice.vaultRedundancy:a: Locally redundant storage keeps three copies of the data in a single datacenter and protects against rack and drive failures only, so it gives no protection against the loss of an availability zone and does not meet the requirement.
perChoice.vaultRedundancy:b: Geo-redundant storage replicates the data to a paired region, which is what protects against a region-wide outage, but it copies the recovery points outside the East US region and provides no in-region zone resilience.
perChoice.backupSchedule:b: A 6-hour interval is one of the permitted values, but it is not the shortest one, so the gap between recovery points stays wider than the platform team asked for.
perChoice.backupSchedule:c: 12 hours is the top of the recovery point objective range that an hourly schedule allows, so it leaves three times the loss window of the 4-hour interval and fails the requirement for the tightest spacing.
perChoice.backupSchedule:d: A single backup per day means the workload is protected only once a day, so the spacing between recovery points is a full day and the several-times-a-day requirement is not met.
perChoice.criticalOperations:b: Azure Policy assignments evaluate and enforce configuration and compliance on resources; they do not build the approval workflow for critical vault operations, which is the job of Azure Resource Guard.
perChoice.criticalOperations:c: Soft delete only allows recovery points to be recovered after they have been deleted, for a limited window; it neither prevents one administrator from deleting them nor introduces a second approval step.
perChoice.criticalOperations:d: Cross-region restore lets a recovery point be restored in another region; it says nothing about who is allowed to carry out critical operations inside the vault.
